extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars studying Euclidean geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and presents the propositions and lemmas from Euclid's Elements (Books XI–XII) covering relations of parallelepipeds, prisms, pyramids, circles, and similar inscribed polygons; includes statements, corollaries, and proof sketches. Useful for readers working through classical solid geometry theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases of solid parallelepipeds reciprocally proportional to their altitudes (forward direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two solid parallelepipeds are equal, then the bases of the solid parallelepipeds are reciprocally proportional to their altitudes (i.e., as base EH to base NP, so is the altitude of CD to the altitude of AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof distinguishes the case where insisting straight lines (altitudes) are at right angles to the bases and the general case. Uses construction of parallelepipeds on equal or related bases and comparison of solids of same altitude to derive proportionality. Shows by contradiction that unequal altitudes would contradict equality of solids. (This is the forward part of the proposition: equal solids imply bases are reciprocally proportional to altitudes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases of solid parallelepipeds reciprocally proportional to their altitudes (converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bases of two solid parallelepipeds are reciprocally proportional to their altitudes (as base EH to base NP, so is the altitude of CD to the altitude of AB), then the two solids are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: construct auxiliary parallelepipeds so that corresponding altitudes or bases become equal or comparable; reduce to case of parallelepipeds whose insisting straight lines are perpendicular to bases (already proved). Uses equal bases and equal altitudes to deduce equality of solids. Handles both right-angle and oblique cases by dropping perpendiculars to base planes and applying earlier results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV — Equal elevated lines produce equal angles in connecting lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the vertices of two equal plane angles two straight lines are elevated above the planes making equal angles with the sides (each to each), and from any points on those elevated lines perpendiculars be dropped to the planes and joined to the vertices, then the straight lines so joined contain equal angles with the elevated straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: copy segments, draw parallels and perpendiculars, then compare triangles to show equalities. The proof produces auxiliary right-angled triangles and uses angle-side-angle (or triangle congruence) and equality of corresponding sides to conclude AB = DE, AG = DF, etc., and thereby equal angles in the constructed triangles. Corollary: if the elevated straight lines are equal, the perpendiculars from their extremities to the planes are equal. An alternative demonstration uses equality of the solid angles and coincidence under application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. XXXV — Perpendiculars from equal elevated lines are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the vertices of two equal plane angles there are elevated two equal straight lines containing equal angles with the sides (each to each), then the perpendiculars from the extremities of those equal straight lines to the planes are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given by observing that the solid angles coincide upon application; equal elevated lines thus have extremities that coincide and their perpendiculars to the corresponding planes coincide, hence are equal. An alternative proof is supplied in the text using congruence of solid angles and coincidence arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI — Three proportional lines: solid parallelepiped equals equilateral parallelepiped from mean proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: If three straight lines are proportionals (A : B = B : C), then the solid parallelepiped described from A, B, C as its three sides is equal to the equilateral parallelepiped described from the mean proportional B, equiangular to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct two solids with equal plane angles and make corresponding sides equal to given segments so that sides about equal angles are reciprocally proportional; show bases equal and altitudes equal (per Prop. XXXV), hence solids equal. The argument reduces the general parallelepiped to one equiangular to it and uses equality of base and altitude to conclude equality of volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII — Four proportionals give proportionals of described similar solids (and converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four straight lines are proportionals (AB : CD = EF : GH), then the similar solid parallelepipeds similarly described from them are proportionals (AK : CL = EM : GN). Conversely, if the similar parallelepipeds similarly described from four straight lines are proportionals, then the straight lines are proportionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses construction of continued proportionals and properties that relate ratios of edges to ratios of corresponding solids (by earlier propositions). For the converse, constructs an auxiliary solid similar to one of the given solids and uses equality of homologous sides to deduce the proportionality of the original lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII — Perpendicular from a point in one plane to another meets common section
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane CD is perpendicular to plane AB and AD is their common section, then the perpendicular drawn from any point E in plane CD to plane AB will meet plane AB on the common section AD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume the foot lies elsewhere, construct perpendiculars in AB to AD, join points and derive two right angles in the same triangle, obtaining contradiction. Concludes that the perpendicular must fall on the common intersection of the planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIX — Division of opposite faces of parallelepiped halves common section and diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: In a solid parallelepiped, if the sides of two opposite planes are each divided into two equal parts, then the common section of the (constructed) planes passing through those division points and the diameter of the parallelepiped cut each other into two equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide opposite faces at midpoints, join corresponding points to form planar sections; show pairs of triangles are equal by parallelism and congruence arguments; deduce that the intersection of the section and the space diagonal bisects both the diagonal and the section. The proof uses alternation of parallel lines, equal halves, and triangle congruence to reach the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XL — Equality of triangular prisms when one base parallelogram is double other triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangular prisms have the same altitude, one has a parallelogram base and the other a triangular base, and the parallelogram is double the triangle, then the two prisms are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete solids to parallelepipeds on those bases; use that parallelepipeds on equal bases and of same altitude are equal, and note that each prism is half of the corresponding parallelepiped. Hence equality follows when one base is double the other triangle's corresponding parallelogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma I (Book XII) — Repeatedly taking more than half eventually yields remainder smaller than a given magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the greater of two unequal magnitudes one repeatedly takes more than its half (and from successive remainders again more than half, etc.), at length there will remain a magnitude less than the least of the proposed magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by comparing the greater magnitude to a multiple of the smaller, partitioning that multiple into equal parts equal to the smaller magnitude, and matching the number of taken parts. Uses the fact that successive 'more-than-half' remainders shrink faster than equal partition remainders, so eventually a remainder is smaller than the given lesser magnitude. Notes same holds if exactly halves are taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book XII Prop. I — Similar polygons inscribed in circles proportional to squares of diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar polygons inscribed in circles are to one another as the squares of their diameters (i.e., polygon areas scale as the square of the diameter of the circumscribed circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: divide polygons into similar triangles; relate corresponding triangles via central/inscribed angles and right triangles involving diameters; use duplicate (square) ratios: as BM to GN so BA to GF, then duplicate ratio gives square(BM):square(GN) equals polygon:polygon. Uses properties of inscribed angles and similar triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book XII Prop. II — Circles proportional to squares of their diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Circles are to one another as the squares of their diameters (i.e., circle areas are proportional to the square of diameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume square(BD):square(FH) corresponds to circle ABCD : some different space; construct polygons approximating circles and use the previous lemma (repeated halving lemma) to reach contradictions about greater/less relations. Shows neither greater nor lesser alternative is possible, hence the ratio is exactly that of squared diameters. Note: the text remarks existence of a fourth proportional for some comparisons and how to interpret that device in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book XII Prop. III — Triangular pyramid can be divided into two equal similar pyramids and two prisms exceeding half
rubrics_metrics.description: Every pyramid having a triangular base may be divided into two equal and similar pyramids (each similar to the whole) and into two equal prisms which together are greater than half the whole pyramid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect edges of base and vertex-to-base segments, join midpoints to form parallelograms and smaller triangles; demonstrate equalities and parallelisms to establish corresponding smaller pyramids are equal and similar to each other and to the whole. Then identify two equal prisms inside whose combined volume exceeds half the pyramid using the constructed subdivisions and parallelogram relations.
